claims.text: Elevated temperatures and irradiation cause an untreated W–Cu composite to exhibit phase separation and interfacial void formation.
Pre-coating tungsten particles or ligaments with electroless nickel before consolidation can produce a thin nickel interlayer at W–Cu interfaces.
The nickel interlayer remains stable and continuous during composite processing, thermal cycling, and irradiation.
The nickel layer acts as a diffusion barrier at W–Cu interfaces.
The nickel layer enhances wetting between tungsten and copper.
The nickel layer reduces W–Cu interfacial energy.
Reduced interfacial energy stabilizes the W–Cu interface under thermal and irradiation stress.
The nickel interlayer suppresses interdiffusion-driven phase separation.
The nickel interlayer reduces interfacial void formation.
Preserving interfacial integrity and reducing void content improves the composite's thermal conductivity.
A nickel-coated W–Cu composite will have higher thermal conductivity than an otherwise identically processed untreated composite after thermal cycling and irradiation.
Phase separation and interfacial voids degrade the thermal conductivity of untreated W–Cu composites.
The proposed benefit applies under powder-metallurgy processing and joint-relevant temperature cycling and irradiation conditions.
Controlled ion-beam irradiation can simulate neutron damage relevant to the intended W-based plasma-facing material/Cu-based cooling component joint.
The magnitude of the conductivity improvement and long-term durability under actual service irradiation have not been quantitatively validated.
